cf.title: Propagate LIMIT bound through the outer side of left join

input.subject: Propagate LIMIT bound through the outer side of left join

verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection is fatal, and neither would stop a review at its level. maintenance-fit-1 is the decisive one: the bound is safe only while NestLoop and MergeJoin never fetch more outer tuples than they return, and the prose names no guard for that. demand-1 asks for evidence beyond one generated-table example. Both are fixable, but the thread has only the author's two messages and the code was not read.

brief.title: Propagate LIMIT bound through the outer side of left and full joins
brief.problem: ExecSetTupleBound() passes a LIMIT bound down to a Sort node for a bounded top-N sort, but stops at any join. So a query like `select ... from (select ... order by x) s left join b ... limit 10` fully sorts the outer input. The author targets queries with LIMIT over a LEFT or FULL join with a sorted outer side.
brief.proposed_design: At executor start, ExecSetTupleBound() passes the bound unchanged to the outer side of a LEFT or FULL NestLoop or MergeJoin. Such a join emits at least one tuple per outer tuple before fetching the next one. The patch applies this only when the join has no qual on its output, and v3 skips HashJoin because a multi-batch hash join can fetch more outer tuples than it returns.
author_claims: The example query runs in about 32.6 ms patched against 63.8 ms on master after warm-up.
The feature is independent of the earlier Top-N sort propagation thread and has its own benefit.
Merge join is the most likely beneficiary, so most new regression tests force a merge join.
Bounded sort can lose to quicksort when the query needs most input tuples, but the existing 'tuples > 2 × limit' costing already accepts this trade-off.
A LEFT or FULL NestLoop or MergeJoin with no output qual never asks its outer side for more tuples than it returns.
brief.thread_state: Only the author has posted, with v2 and then v3, which drops HashJoin. No reviewer has replied yet.
unclear: The material does not say whether the planner's costs change, so EXPLAIN estimates may not match the bounded execution.
The patch does not say how it treats joins with join quals versus other quals, or semi and anti joins.
The thread gives one benchmark and no case where the bounded sort is slower than master.
The material does not say whether parallel plans, Gather, or Memoize nodes on the outer side get the bound.
The patch does not say what happens to the bound on rescan of a NestLoop or MergeJoin under a parameterized path.

prior_attempts.title: Pass down Limit bounds [take-2]
prior_attempts.quote: I think ps_numTuples should be int64.
prior_attempts.reason: Reviewers asked for changes. ps_numTuples should be a 64-bit type, and 0 should mean "unknown" so most nodes need not set the field. Robert Haas also asked the patch to keep planning-time use of constant LIMIT values separate from the execution-time mechanism. The author said he would revise the patch, but no revised version appears in the visible messages before the entry was returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P6 added a new PlanState field to carry a Limit hint to child nodes and to postgres_fdw. This proposal adds no field or API; it extends the existing ExecSetTupleBound() through the outer side of LEFT and FULL NestLoop and MergeJoin.

objections.title: Correctness rests on an unenforced fetch-order property of join nodes
objections.failure_scenario: A later patch changes NestLoop or MergeJoin so that it reads outer tuples ahead, for example batched outer fetches or new prefetching. The bounded Sort below then returns only N tuples while the join needs more, and the query silently returns fewer rows. No test or assertion catches this until a user reports wrong results.
objections.argument: The commit message bases the whole optimization on one property: a LEFT/FULL NestLoop or MergeJoin never fetches more outer tuples than it returns. A bounded Sort cuts off its output at the bound, so a violation gives wrong results, not just lost speed. v3 already had to drop HashJoin because multi-batch mode breaks this property (message #2), which shows how easily join code can break it. The prose does not say whether the patch adds a comment or an Assert in the join nodes so that a future change there fails loudly.
objections.author_must_show: How will a future change to NestLoop or MergeJoin outer fetching be detected as breaking this bound, through an Assert, a runtime check, or a test that fails?

critic.reasoning: ExecSetTupleBound() already relies on unasserted properties of other nodes, but a join's fetch order is subtler, and v3 dropped HashJoin for breaking it. A bounded Sort truncates its output, so a later violation gives wrong results, and the prose names no guard.

objections.title: Demand rests on one synthetic query shape
objections.failure_scenario: A committer takes on a new executor contract: a LEFT or FULL NestLoop or MergeJoin must never fetch more outer tuples than it returns. The material shows no production query that gains from it. If the contract later breaks for a join that gains new behaviour, users get wrong LIMIT results, and the benefit was never shown outside a test.
objections.argument: The only evidence is the generated-table example in message #1, about 64 ms against 33 ms. That example puts ORDER BY in a subquery and LIMIT outside it with no top-level ORDER BY, which is not how users usually write top-N queries. No field report, -general or -bugs thread, or second user appears, and no reviewer has replied (messages #1 and #2). The author also notes that bounded sort can be slower than quicksort, and no case measures that slowdown.
objections.author_must_show: Which real query shapes, such as a top-level order by over a merge left join, gain from this, and how often do they appear in practice?

critic.reasoning: The thread shows one generated-table example, no slowdown measurement and no second voice. Its wrong-results risk repeats maintenance-fit-1 and adds no weight here; the cost is otherwise small, so evidence of common plan shapes that gain would answer it.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: ExecSetTupleBound() now depends on NestLoop and MergeJoin never fetching more outer tuples than they return.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: A Sort below a LEFT or FULL join under LIMIT becomes a bounded sort, which the author says can lose to quicksort.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: see objection demand-1: Demand rests on one synthetic query shape

questions: How will a future change to outer-tuple fetching in NestLoop or MergeJoin be caught: by an Assert, a runtime check, or a regression test that fails?
Which query shapes that users write, such as a top-level order by with limit over a merge left join, gain from this patch?
What is the measured slowdown against master when the bounded sort is chosen but the query needs most of the outer tuples?
What happens to the bound when the join is rescanned, or when Gather, Gather Merge or Memoize sits between the join and the Sort?
Which quals block the bound: only quals on the join output, or also join quals, and are semi and anti joins excluded?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the executor's join nodes and tuplesort's bounded mode; none has posted in the thread.
committability.liability: The owner signs for wrong LIMIT results if NestLoop or MergeJoin ever starts to read outer tuples ahead, for as long as this propagation exists.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v3 five days after v2 and removed HashJoin after finding the multi-batch problem without a reviewer's prompt.

priority.reason: The patch touches one executor file plus regression tests and adds no user-visible surface, so review is cheap. The thread shows one generated-table example, and the fetch-order property of the join nodes needs care in later join work.

provisional_note: Without the code, nobody can confirm which quals block the bound, how rescans and parallel or Memoize nodes behave, or whether the join nodes carry a comment or Assert for the fetch-order property.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix out-of-bounds with function PQescapeInternal
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the buffer size that PQescapeInternal in libpq allocates on its slow path, adding two bytes per quote or backslash. It followed a Coverity report of an out-of-bounds write in pg_createsubscriber.c.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane replied that each quote or backslash is already counted in input_len, so one extra byte per character is enough. He added an Assert that the buffer is filled exactly, and check-world passed. The author checked with a debugger, found no overrun, called the Coverity warning wrong, and withdrew the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Nonsense.  The quote or backslash is already counted in input_len,
so we need to add just one more.

precedents_retrieved.title: Memory-bounded HashAgg
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets HashAgg spill to disk so it stays within work_mem even when the planner underestimates the number of groups. When memory is full, existing groups keep aggregating, tuples for new groups go to partition files, and each file is processed in a later pass. A GUC, enable_hashagg_disk, lets the planner choose HashAgg even when it expects the hash table to exceed memory.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Tomas Vondra argued for hashjoin-like batching and noted that growing transition states such as array_agg are not handled, but in message #38 he called the approach reasonable. The last message says the discussion moved to another thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Table Partition + Join Pushdown
precedents_retrieved.summary: When a hash join has a partitioned (inheritance) table on one side, the planner would push the join below the Append, joining each child separately. Each child's CHECK constraint is rewritten through the join clause into a filter on the other relation, so each per-child hash table holds fewer rows.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas pointed out that a CHECK(P(x)) constraint on A does not mean that only rows with P(y) true can join when A.x = B.y, because equality under the join operator need not mean equality for all purposes. For numeric, 1 and 1.0 are equal but differ under length(x::text), so the derived filter can drop matching rows. He said the whole patch rests on this idea, and suggested hash partitioning with the opclass hash function as the safe way to get the same optimization.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The fundamental problem is that equality according to the join
operator need not mean equality for all purposes.  1 and 1.0, as
numerics, are equal, but not the same.

precedents_retrieved.title: Range Merge Join
precedents_retrieved.summary: Extend the existing Merge Join executor node to also handle range conditions (containment @> / <@ between a range and an element, or scalar BETWEEN-AND / paired inequalities), optionally combined with equality conditions, by adding a range_cond alongside the merge_cond and extending the merge join state machine. The planner would detect such conditions and use estimates to choose this "Range Merge Join" over other strategies.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tomas Vondra's review found that the patch still did not compile with asserts, had no regression tests exercising the new code, and lacked comments explaining the new functions and the reworked executor blocks. Two months later Julien Rouhaud asked whether the author planned to continue; no response from the author is visible before the entry was returned with feedback. Earlier, Jeff Davis had raised concerns about multiple join keys and suggested a CustomScan extension, which the authors declined.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I took a brief look at the patch, and I think there are two main issues
preventing it from moving forward.

precedents_retrieved.title: Support empty ranges with bounds information
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch keeps the bounds of empty ranges built from bounds, such as int4range(6,6,'[)'), and returns them from lower() and upper(). A v2 patch restored lower() and upper() and added range_start() and range_end() to expose the stored bounds instead.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the patch breaks the set-theoretic definition of ranges as sets of points, to support a regexp_positions use case. Mark Dilger showed that the changed RANGE_HAS_LBOUND and RANGE_HAS_UBOUND macros make hash_range() give different hashes for empty ranges that compare equal, so even v2 changes semantics. Fixing the hash would leave visibly different values comparing equal, so the author abandoned the patch.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
We had a clean set-theoretic
definition of ranges as sets of points, and with this we would not.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pass down Limit bounds [take-2]
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a ps_numTuples field to PlanState, which a parent node such as Limit sets before the first ExecProcNode() so child nodes can treat it as a hint and pass it further down. As an example, postgres_fdw uses the hint to add a LIMIT to the remote query when ORDER BY is pushed down.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers asked for changes. ps_numTuples should be a 64-bit type, and 0 should mean "unknown" so most nodes need not set the field. Robert Haas also asked the patch to keep planning-time use of constant LIMIT values separate from the execution-time mechanism. The author said he would revise the patch, but no revised version appears in the visible messages before the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I think ps_numTuples should be int64.

precedents_retrieved.title: Document efficient self-joins / UPDATE LIMIT techniques.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds documentation examples that show how to update or delete rows in batches, using a CTE with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and `LIMIT` and a self-join on the system column `ctid`. It offers this as a documented workaround while `UPDATE` and `DELETE` have no `LIMIT` clause.

His comments covered redundant examples, the stated rationale and wording. Corey Huinker then sent a revised patch, and Laurenz Albe judged it close to ready for committer. The author had reopened the entry in the commitfest that was already closed, so Laurenz Albe closed it again and moved the patch to a new entry in the open commitfest.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add a greedy join search algorithm to handle large join problems
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds GOO (Greedy Operator Ordering), a greedy join search that repeatedly merges the legal join pair with the lowest estimated cost until one join remains. It is meant to replace GEQO for large join problems, enabled by `enable_goo_join_search` above geqo_threshold.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. On the withdrawal date the author posted v5 with plans for broader plan-quality tests and a hybrid greedy/DP approach. Tomas Vondra had said earlier that picking locally optimal joins is a flaw built into any greedy method.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert support for improved tracking of nested queries
Reverted commit(s): Track more precisely query locations for nested statements; Fix regression with location calculation of nested statements; pg_stat_statements: Add tests for nested queries with level tracking
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This commit reverts the two following commits:
- 499edb09741b, track more precisely query locations for nested
statements.
- 06450c7b8c70, a follow-up fix of 499edb09741b with query locations.
The test introduced in this commit is not reverted.  This is proving
useful to track a problem that only pgaudit was able to detect.

These prove to have issues with the tracking of SELECT statements, when
these use multiple parenthesis which is something supported by the
grammar.  Incorrect location and lengths are causing pg_stat_statements
to become confused, failing its job in query normalization with
potential out-of-bound writes because the location and the length may
not match with what can be handled.  A lot of the query patterns
discussed when this issue was reported have no test coverage in the main
regression test suite, or the recovery test 027_stream_regress.pl would
have caught the problems as pg_stat_statements is loaded by the node
running the regression tests.  A first step would be to improve the test
coverage to stress more the query normalization logic.

A different portion of this work was done in 45e0ba30fc40, with the
addition of tests for nested queries.  These can be left in the tree.
They are useful to track the way inner queries are currently tracked by
PGSS with non-top-level entries, and will be useful when reconsidering
in the future the work reverted here.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent gives a rejection reason that still applies. P6 was returned over its field type, a sentinel value and the split between planning and execution, and an executor-only extension of ExecSetTupleBound() raises none of these. Message #1 links an earlier Top-N sort propagation thread and calls this a separate feature; the visible material does not say how that thread ended.

The patch only changes how the executor passes an existing LIMIT bound, and it adds no syntax, keyword, GUC, catalog object, pg_dump state or psql change. Visible effects are EXPLAIN ANALYZE showing top-N heapsort instead of a full sort, and possibly a different order for tied sort keys under a LIMIT without a top-level ORDER BY, which is already unspecified. Bounded sorts below Limit work this way today.

The patch changes only executor-time propagation in ExecSetTupleBound() plus regression tests. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or replication state. PlanState fields are reused, so no extension ABI change is visible from the material; the code would need to confirm this.

The patch adds no object, privilege, setting or monitoring output. It only lets fewer outer tuples be read and sorted under a LIMIT, so no user can see or run more than on master. Security barrier and RLS quals on the join output block the bound, since the patch requires no qual there. Whether quals below the join can still leak was not checked without the code.
The change is small, sits in execProcnode.c, and adds no cost for queries without LIMIT. No committer has engaged yet. That affects committability and is not counted against the design.

No existing feature gives this result automatically. A user can move the LIMIT into the outer subquery by hand, but that needs a rewrite, which ORM-generated queries may not allow. The patch also extends the existing ExecSetTupleBound() mechanism rather than adding a second one, and an extension cannot change this executor path.
Cost to non-users looks small, since the change is limited to execProcnode.c and does not touch the planner. The only gap is evidence of demand beyond one synthetic example.
